title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
blurb: Give LLMs real, current knowledge grounded in your own data.

lessons.title: The RAG pipeline
lessons.explain: RAG solves the LLM's stale/unknown-data problem: split your docs into chunks, embed them into vectors, store them, then for each query retrieve the most similar chunks and feed them to the LLM so its answer is grounded.
lessons.example:
docs -> chunk -> embed -> vector DB
query -> embed -> top-k similar -> LLM(query+chunks)
objectives: Trace how RAG retrieves and grounds generation in your own documents

commonMistakes: Skipping evaluation of the retrieval step specifically -- a wrong final answer might stem from bad retrieval, not bad generation.

lessons.title: Document ingestion & chunking strategies
objectives: Explain how documents are prepared and split for retrieval
Explain how ingestion changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ingestion with chunking and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before documents can be searched, they must be ingested (loaded from PDFs, web pages, databases) and chunked — split into smaller pieces, since embedding and retrieving an entire long document as one unit loses precision (you'd retrieve the whole thing even if only one paragraph is relevant).
examples:
# naive chunking: split every 500 characters, ignoring sentence/paragraph boundaries
# better: split on natural boundaries (paragraphs, sections), with some overlap between
# chunks so a fact split across a boundary isn't completely lost
commonMistakes: Chunking purely by a fixed character count with no regard for sentence or paragraph boundaries — this routinely splits a single coherent idea across two chunks, weakening retrieval for.
lessons.careerRelevance: Chunking strategy is one of the highest-leverage, most commonly tuned decisions in any real RAG system's quality.

lessons.title: Embeddings & vector databases
objectives: Explain how chunks become searchable by meaning, not just keywords
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: cosine similarity.
Explain how embeddings changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example

lessons.explanation: Each chunk is converted into an embedding — a dense vector where semantically similar text ends up close together in vector space (as covered in the NLP track).
examples:
chunk_embedding = embed_model.encode(chunk_text)   # e.g. a 768-dimension vector
vector_db.insert(chunk_id, chunk_embedding, metadata={'source': doc_name})
# later: find chunks whose embeddings are CLOSEST to the query's embedding
commonMistakes: Assuming any database can efficiently do this kind of similarity search at scale — specialized indexing structures (like HNSW) are what make searching millions of vectors fast; this is.
lessons.careerRelevance: Vector databases are now a standard, expected piece of infrastructure in any real production RAG system. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Similarity search, metadata filtering & query transformation
objectives: Combine semantic search with metadata filters and query rewriting
Explain how metadata filtering changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect metadata filtering with query transformation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Similarity search alone finds semantically similar chunks — but real systems usually also filter by metadata (date range, source, access permissions) to narrow results to what's actually eligible. Query transformation rewrites or expands the user's original query before searching — e.g.
examples:
# metadata filtering: search only documents where source='official_docs' AND date > '2025-01-01'
# query transformation: user asks 'what about the pricing?' (vague, needs context)
# -> rewritten to 'What is the pricing for the Enterprise plan?' using prior conversation turns
commonMistakes: Searching with the user's raw, under-specified follow-up question with no context-aware rewriting — this frequently retrieves irrelevant chunks because the query alone doesn't capture what's.
lessons.careerRelevance: Query transformation is a frequently underestimated lever for RAG quality, often mattering as much as the retrieval algorithm itself.

lessons.title: Reranking & context construction
objectives: Explain why an initial retrieval pass is often reranked, and how final context is assembled
Explain how reranking changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect reranking with two-stage retrieval and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Initial similarity search (fast, approximate) often returns a broader set of candidate chunks than needed; a reranking step (using a slower but more accurate model) reorders these candidates by true relevance to the specific query, improving precision at the cost of some extra latency.
examples:
candidates = vector_search(query, top_k=50)     # fast, broad first pass
reranked = rerank_model(query, candidates)        # slower, more accurate reordering
final_context = format_top_n(reranked, n=5)        # assemble what actually goes in the prompt
commonMistakes: Sending all 50 initially-retrieved chunks directly to the LLM without reranking or trimming — this wastes context budget on lower-relevance chunks and can bury the truly relevant ones.
lessons.careerRelevance: The retrieve-then-rerank pattern is a standard, expected architecture in production-quality RAG systems.

lessons.title: Grounded generation & citation design
objectives: Design prompts and system behavior for grounded, citable generation
Explain how grounded generation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect grounded generation with citation attribution and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Grounded generation explicitly instructs the model to answer ONLY using the retrieved context provided (not its general pretrained knowledge), and to say it doesn't know when the retrieved context doesn't contain the answer — directly fighting hallucination.
examples:
# grounding instruction: 'Answer ONLY using the provided context below.
# If the context doesn't contain the answer, say you don't know. Cite the source for each claim.'
# -- without this explicit instruction, the model may blend in ungrounded pretrained knowledge
commonMistakes: Assuming retrieval alone guarantees grounded answers — without an EXPLICIT instruction to use only the provided context, the model can still blend in unrelated pretrained knowledge alongside.
lessons.careerRelevance: Citation design is frequently the single most trust-building feature in a real RAG product, letting users verify rather than just trust.

lessons.title: Retrieval & generation evaluation
objectives: Evaluate a RAG system's retrieval quality and final answer quality separately
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: Recall@K, MRR (mean reciprocal rank).
Explain how retrieval evaluation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect retrieval evaluation with generation evaluation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: RAG systems need TWO separate evaluations: retrieval evaluation (did we find the right chunks? measured with metrics like hit rate or recall against a labeled set of query-to-correct-document pairs) and generation evaluation (given good chunks, did the model produce a good, grounded, accurate answer?).
examples:
# retrieval eval: for 50 labeled test queries, does the retrieved set contain the KNOWN correct document?
# generation eval (given GOOD retrieved chunks): is the final answer accurate, grounded, and well-cited?
# -- always debug these two stages SEPARATELY, not as one combined 'is the answer good' check
commonMistakes: Debugging a bad RAG answer by only looking at the final output — always check whether retrieval found the right chunks FIRST, before assuming the problem is in generation.
lessons.careerRelevance: This two-stage evaluation discipline is exactly what separates a systematically-improvable RAG system from one tuned by guesswork. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Freshness, access control & common failure modes
objectives: Identify practical operational concerns and common RAG failure patterns
Explain how index freshness changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect index freshness with access control enforcement and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Real RAG systems need a plan for freshness (how often is the underlying document index updated as source documents change) and access control (a user should only ever retrieve chunks from documents they're actually permitted to see — a critical, easy-to-miss security requirement, not an afterthought).
examples:
# access control failure (serious): a shared vector index with no permission filtering means
# ANY user's query could retrieve chunks from documents they shouldn't have access to at all
# -- metadata filtering by user/team permissions must be enforced at retrieval time, always
commonMistakes: Building a shared vector index without permission-aware filtering baked into every retrieval call — this is a real, serious security gap, not a minor edge case.
lessons.careerRelevance: Access control in RAG systems is now a standard, explicit requirement in any enterprise-facing AI product review.

lessons.title: When RAG is (and isn't) the right approach
objectives: Decide when RAG genuinely solves the problem at hand
Explain how when to use RAG changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect when to use RAG with document-dependent answers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: RAG is well-suited when answers depend on specific, current, or proprietary documents a model wasn't trained on. It's a poor fit when the task needs general reasoning rather than document lookup, or when the true answer isn't actually contained in any retrievable document -- RAG can't invent grounding that doesn't exist in the corpus.
examples:
# good RAG fit: 'What does OUR company's return policy say about X?'
# poor RAG fit: 'Write a creative poem about autumn'
# (nothing to retrieve -- this needs generation, not lookup)
commonMistakes: Reaching for RAG by default for every task, even ones that don't actually depend on retrievable documents at all.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly scoping when RAG applies (vs prompting alone, or an agent) is a real, practical architecture decision.

lessons.title: Hybrid Search: Combining Dense and Sparse Retrieval
objectives: Explain why combining dense (embedding-based) and sparse (keyword-based) retrieval catches more relevant results than either alone
Explain how hybrid search changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect hybrid search with dense retrieval and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Dense retrieval (embeddings + vector similarity) is good at capturing MEANING -- it can find a relevant passage even if it doesn't share exact wording with the query. But it can miss exact matches that matter, like a specific product ID, error code, or rare technical term, since embeddings represent overall semantic meaning, not precise token identity.
examples:
# Dense retrieval alone: might miss an exact match for a specific error code
# if the surrounding wording differs a lot from the query's phrasing

# Sparse (BM25) retrieval alone: would nail the exact error code match,
# but might miss a conceptually relevant passage that doesn't use the
# same words as the query

# Hybrid: run both retrievers, combine/rerank their results --
# catches the exact-match case AND the semantic-similarity case
commonMistakes: Assuming dense (embedding-based) retrieval alone is always sufficient -- it's genuinely weak at exact matches (IDs, codes, rare terms) precisely because embeddings capture overall meaning.
lessons.careerRelevance: Production RAG systems handling real, varied queries commonly use hybrid search specifically because relying on dense retrieval alone leaves a real, recurring class of queries poorly served.

description: Give LLMs real, current knowledge grounded in your own data.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is it important to evaluate retrieval and generation separately in a RAG system?
interviewPreparation.a: A bad answer could come from retrieving the wrong chunks (a retrieval failure) or from generating poorly despite having the right chunks (a generation failure) -- these need different fixes, and a single combined 'good/bad answer' judgment can't tell you which one actually happened, or where to focus effort.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you use hybrid search instead of pure dense (embedding-based) retrieval?
interviewPreparation.a: When query patterns include exact-match needs (specific IDs, error codes, rare technical terms) that embeddings tend to miss, since dense retrieval captures overall meaning rather than precise token identity -- combining it with keyword/BM25-style sparse retrieval catches both the semantic matches and the exact matches.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide on a chunking strategy for a new document set?
interviewPreparation.a: Base it on the actual document structure and how people will query it -- dense technical documents with numbered sections often benefit from larger, structure-aware chunks, while shorter, more atomic content might chunk well at a smaller size. There's no universal right chunk size, only one justified by the specific documents and queries.

interviewPreparation.q: A RAG system retrieves topically-related but unhelpful passages for a factual question. How do you diagnose this?
interviewPreparation.a: Check whether the chunking is fragmenting relevant information awkwardly, whether the embedding model captures the right kind of similarity for this domain, and whether metadata filtering or reranking could help surface more specific matches -- it's rarely one single cause, so isolating which stage is actually failing matters.

interviewPreparation.q: When is RAG NOT the right approach for a given problem?
interviewPreparation.a: When the task doesn't actually depend on document-grounded facts -- creative writing, general reasoning, or tasks where the model's own broad knowledge is sufficient don't benefit from retrieval, and adding RAG in those cases adds complexity and latency without solving a real problem.

careerApplications: A concrete, in-demand AI engineering skill beyond just prompting.

capstone.title: Build a production-minded RAG system, with a measured evaluation of retrieval and generation separately
capstone.description: Take a real document set and build a genuinely production-minded RAG pipeline: chunking justified by the document type, a retrieval strategy (dense, or hybrid if the query patterns call for it), reranking, grounded generation with real citations, and -- critically -- separate evaluation of retrieval quality and generation quality, since a good answer built on the wrong retrieved chunks is not the same success as a good answer built on the right ones. This assumes tokens, embeddings, and context windows are already understood -- the focus here is retrieval system design and measurement, not LLM fundamentals.
deliverables: A chunking strategy justified by the actual document type (not a default chunk size picked without reasoning)
A retrieval approach -- dense, or hybrid if you can justify why pure dense retrieval would miss real query patterns for this document set
Grounded generation with real citations pointing to the actual retrieved source, not fabricated or generic references
Separate evaluation of retrieval quality (are the right chunks being found) and generation quality (is the answer good given those chunks) -- not one combined 'does it work' judgment
A written account of one real failure mode you found (a topically-related-but-unhelpful retrieval, a stale index, or a case RAG genuinely isn't well suited for) and how you'd address or accept it
capstone.portfolioTips: Separating retrieval evaluation from generation evaluation is the single detail that most distinguishes a real RAG system from a demo -- it's the difference between 'the answer looked right' and being able to say specifically whether retrieval or generation is the actual bottleneck when something goes wrong.

industryUsage.usage: Uses RAG-style retrieval over user workspaces to ground AI answers in a user's actual documents, where citation accuracy and retrieval quality directly affect user trust.
Built its entire product around grounded, cited generation -- retrieval quality and citation accuracy are the core product, not a peripheral feature.
Applies retrieval-augmented approaches to ground AI features in proprietary or frequently-changing content, where index freshness and access control are real, practical production concerns.
